title: BradEngine

contributors.contribution: Jamie built BradEngine partly as a platform for teaching his two sons programming. They used it together to build games, multiplayer demos, physics experiments, and other learning projects.

description:
I built BradEngine as a reusable JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas game engine and used it extensively to teach my two sons real game-programming concepts through hands-on projects. Instead of hiding complexity behind a simplified educational framework, they worked with the same engine lifecycle, rendering, physics, networking, and reusable systems I was developing. Together we built games and multiplayer demos using WebRTC and PeerJS, while the engine also grew to support my own 3D, voxel, physics, AI, and simulation experiments. BradEngine became an important architectural precursor to GameEngineTS.

View the source and demos on GitHub

sections.title: A Real Engine for Teaching
paragraphs: I built BradEngine partly as a practical environment for teaching my two sons programming and game development.

Rather than creating a simplified educational tool, I taught with the same reusable engine systems, classes, lifecycle, rendering, input, physics, and networking concepts used by the projects themselves.

sections.title: Learning by Building Games
paragraphs: The teaching approach was project-driven: we used BradEngine to build playable games, technical demos, and small experiments together.
This let my sons learn how individual programming concepts fit into a larger application architecture instead of treating each topic as an isolated exercise.

sections.title: Reusable Engine Architecture
paragraphs: BradEngine moved common application and game responsibilities into reusable systems so individual projects could focus on their own behavior.
Projects were assembled from cooperating classes and shared services rather than one large procedural script.

sections.title: Level Lifecycle
paragraphs: Levels followed a shared lifecycle abstraction with focused responsibilities that made the structure of a running game explicit.

sections.title: Resource & Runtime Support
paragraphs: The engine provided shared media loading and project configuration so examples could reuse common infrastructure.
Projects could configure display size, debugging, networking, frame rate, physics timing, and script loading.

sections.title: WebRTC Multiplayer
paragraphs: WebRTC / PeerJS networking became a native BradEngine feature rather than a one-off experiment.
My sons used the networking support with me to build and run multiplayer games and demos across separate computers, giving them direct experience with real peer-to-peer game communication.

sections.title: Canvas, Physics & Gameplay
paragraphs: HTML5 Canvas was the main rendering surface, supporting 2D games, UI, particles, diagnostics, and composited visual layers.
BradEngine also supported homemade collision experiments and established physics libraries such as Box2D and Cannon.js, which gave us additional systems to use in teaching projects.

sections.title: 3D Engine Work
paragraphs: BradEngine later grew a native software 3D renderer with its own meshes, cameras, projection, lighting, terrain, height maps, and related systems.
That graphics work became substantial enough to have its own dedicated portfolio card.

sections.title: Voxel World System
paragraphs: The engine also supported a dedicated voxel subsystem with chunked procedural terrain, Web Worker generation, mesh construction, streaming, persistence, and runtime editing.
The voxel work likewise has its own portfolio card.

sections.title: Experimental Systems
paragraphs: I also used BradEngine independently as a technical laboratory for studying unfamiliar concepts such as neural networks, evolutionary algorithms, cellular automata, physics, and simulation.
Those experiments are documented in the separate BradEngine Experimental Systems Lab card so this umbrella card can remain focused on the engine and its teaching role.

sections.title: Teaching Through Real Systems
paragraphs: The most important teaching idea behind BradEngine was that my sons worked with real software structure rather than a toy abstraction.
They learned by seeing how reusable engine code, game-specific code, graphics, physics, networking, and application lifecycle responsibilities fit together in working projects.

sections.title: Basic Reusable Application Designer
paragraphs: The name BradEngine came from my son's name and the backronym Basic Reusable Application Designer.
The name started playfully, but the engine's emphasis on reusable systems ultimately made the description surprisingly accurate.

sections.title: Precursor to GameEngineTS
paragraphs: BradEngine became an important architectural ancestor of GameEngineTS.
Both emphasize reusable systems, explicit lifecycle responsibilities, modular project code, and reducing the amount of project-specific programming needed to assemble a game.
GameEngineTS later formalized and significantly expanded ideas that were already emerging here.

historicalNotes: The umbrella BradEngine card should primarily tell the engine-and-teaching story; deep 3D, voxel, and experimental-system details belong on dedicated cards.
Jamie built BradEngine partly to teach his two sons programming and game development through real projects rather than a simplified educational framework.
Jamie and his sons used BradEngine's WebRTC / PeerJS networking to build and run multiplayer games and demos on separate computers.
WebRTC / PeerJS was a reusable native BradEngine feature, not merely an isolated experiment.
Jamie's sons participated as student developers / game prototype developers in the broader BradEngine teaching projects.
Jamie's ANN, evolutionary, cellular-automata, and physics learning experiments were his own work and belong primarily on the Experimental Systems Lab card.
The custom software 3D renderer and voxel engine are substantial enough to remain separate portfolio cards.
BradEngine development began in 2019 and continued for approximately three years.
BradEngine expands to Basic Reusable Application Designer and is also a reference to Jamie's son's name.
The platform was used for games, teaching projects, physics demos, networking demos, graphics experiments, machine-learning work, and simulation projects.
BradEngine used a shared src engine folder with examples, learning projects, common media, documentation, and reusable runtime code.
Its lifecycle included loadResources(), setup(), getKeyboardInput(), and update(delta).
The engine supported shared image, sound, font, mesh, and media loading.
The engine supported per-project configuration for display, debug, networking, rendering timing, and physics timing.
The homemade 3D renderer was native to BradEngine.
The 3D pipeline included meshes, cameras, lighting, terrain, height maps, morphing meshes, and voxel chunks.
Voxel terrain generation used Web Workers.
BradEngine included ray-casting and textured-raycasting experiments.
BradEngine included particle systems.
BradEngine included homemade 2D physics/collision work as well as Box2D, Cannon.js, and Three.js experiments.
BradEngine included cloth simulation experiments.
WebRTC / PeerJS multiplayer worked successfully between Jamie and his sons on separate machines.
BradEngine included artificial neural-network and machine-learning examples including XOR, graph/training, and Pong-related experiments.
BradEngine included cellular-automata implementations including Conway's Game of Life, elementary rule-number experiments, sand simulation, and interactive fire.
The repository includes a broad example ecosystem including 3D Asteroids, Space Boss, Voxel Engine, textured raycasting, cloth physics, Fire Finger, Solar System, Sand Sim, Starfield, and ANN XOR.
The architecture was modular and class-based but was not yet the fully formalized component-oriented architecture later used by GameEngineTS.
BradEngine is a direct architectural precursor to GameEngineTS.
